newsitem.title: CANADA: NOVA considers gas pipeline legal challenge.
newsitem.headline: NOVA considers gas pipeline legal challenge.

text.p: NOVA Corp, girding for a battle against a new pipeline aiming to compete in its exclusive Alberta natural gas transport territory, is considering a possible court challenge, a NOVA spokesman said on Thursday.

NOVA's lawyers could challenge Canadian regulatory authorities or the proposed Palliser Pipeline -- or both -- depending on how the Alberta government rules on the concept of pipeline competition in the province, NOVA's Paul Clark said.

Legal action would also depend on the outcome of the Palliser application, which is currently before Canada's National Energy Board. Palliser is a 1.2-billion cubic feet per day pipeline proposal backed by PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd and Westcoast Energy Inc. It would extend into Saskatchewan from just north of Calgary.

A legal battle is one of a series of options being studied by NOVA unit NOVA Gas Transmission Ltd to fight for a clear reading on how pipelines would compete in Alberta, which regulatory authorities claim jurisdiction and how tolls charged to shippers are levied.
"In the legal group, they're looking at all aspects of the issue and how to approach it," Clark said. "They haven't landed on any particular point of view at this time."

"In the legal group, they're looking at all aspects of the issue and how to approach it," Clark said. "They haven't landed on any particular point of view at this time." NOVA has already said it was devising alternative tariff structures should Palliser be approved, including zone and distance-based tolls.
The onset of new Alberta gas pipeline projects, which are aimed at lowering tolls for some producers by providing competition, has opened a Pandora's box of controversy.

PanCanadian devised Palliser because much of its gas production lies along the proposed southern Alberta route. Currently, under a decades-old toll structure called the "postage stamp" rate, it pays the same to ship gas to the border on the NOVA system as shippers in the northernmost regions of the province.
NOVA has said the postage stamp, which was retained in an Alberta Energy and Utilities Board decision earlier this year, has led to the development of remote gas fields and Alberta's economic growth.

Palliser filed its application with the NEB because it would cross the Alberta-Saskatchewan border. If it was approved, it would be under different authority than NOVA, which is regulated by the AEUB.

"The challenge is based on trying to find a level playing field that NOVA or anyone else can compete on, so we all know he rules for pipelines in Alberta and we can operate our business on these sets of common rules," he said. NOVA Gas Transmission, which moves 12 BCF of gas per day, is currently Alberta's only major gas gathering and transmission network.
Clark said NOVA was calling for the Alberta government to make its position on the issue known soon to ease uncertainty in the industry over the emotional issue.
